author: Abahlali_3
title: South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity
content:
South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity

Address at a public meeting hosted by Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa at the Ellen Melville Centre in Auckland on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Comrades, thank you for inviting me to return to Aotearoa. I bring you greetings of solidarity from Abahlali baseMjondolo, the shack dwellers’ movement of South Africa, which was formed in Durban in 2005 and now has more than 200 000 members across South Africa.

It is fifteen years since I was last here, in 2011, when we commemorated the thirtieth anniversary of the great protests against the Springbok rugby tour of 1981. I want to begin by remembering that history, and by thanking all the people of this country who stood with us against apartheid. People marched, confronted the police, and sometimes faced arrest and violence. You refused to allow the apartheid state to present itself as a normal member of the international community.

This was an outstanding example of international solidarity, and an example that we should seek to emulate in our solidarity with the people of Palestine.

In our movement we speak of living solidarity. This means solidarity that exists in action, not just in words. It means solidarity between people who recognise one another as equals.

Settler colonialism in South Africa and Israel

South Africa and Palestine are both countries that have been oppressed by settler colonialism. This is part of the reason for the long solidarity with Palestine among South Africans.

But there are important differences between these two forms of settler colonialism. In South Africa, the colonial system was organised around the dispossession of Africans from their land, the theft of their cattle and the exploitation of their labour. The economy depended on African workers in the mines, on the farms, in the factories and in the homes of white people. The settlers wanted the land, but they also wanted the labour of the people they had dispossessed.

Huge numbers of people were forced from their homes and land as African people were pushed into ‘reserves’, based on the system used to oppress Native Americans, and later into the ‘Bantustans’, the so-called ‘homelands’. The Bantustans were not just used to confine the African people on tiny bits of land. They were also central to the migrant labour system that ensured cheap labour for white capital and for white families in their homes.

African workers were forced by economic necessity to leave their families and communities to find work in the mines and cities. Many were compelled to live in single-sex hostels, separated from their families. Africans were wanted as workers but rejected as citizens with equal rights. They were systematically dehumanised. This system was maintained through the police, the army, prisons, torture and killing. Those who resisted were treated as criminals and terrorists.

When we look at Palestine today, we recognise many of these methods of oppression. We see a fundamentally racist settler colonial system in which there is ongoing dispossession of people from their land by the Israeli state and settlers. We see homes being demolished. We see communities separated from one another by walls, checkpoints and military restrictions. We see people who stand up against oppression being called ‘terrorists’ and subject to mass imprisonment, torture and murder.

The struggles against racism and for land are central to the struggle for freedom, both in South Africa and in Palestine. But there are also differences between apartheid in South Africa and oppression in Palestine.

While Palestinians have been exploited as workers, the fundamental drive of settler colonialism in Israel is to remove or destroy the Palestinian people rather than to exploit them for their labour.

In South Africa, the apartheid system required the continued presence of a large and hyper-exploited African workforce, while seeking to control, segregate and impoverish it. In Palestine, the settler-colonial project has involved the destruction of Palestinian communities, the removal of Palestinians from their land and the attempt to establish and maintain territorial and political control through their displacement.

The Nakba of 1948 forced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. Many became refugees in other countries, and they and their descendants remain unable to return. The occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967 has brought further dispossession, settlement expansion and military rule. The genocide in Gaza and the ongoing theft of land in the West Bank have continued the process begun with the Nakba.

We must also recognise that the Palestinian experience has become more terrible in certain respects than the experience of apartheid South Africa. The scale of the destruction of Gaza, the mass displacement and the killing of civilians have horrified people across the world.

There were terrible massacres in apartheid South Africa, most notoriously the massacres at Sharpeville in 1960 and Soweto in 1976. The system of oppression was defended with mass imprisonment, torture and murder and a civil war between Inkatha and the United Democratic Front, between Zulu supremacy and a movement for national liberation. We must also always remember the devastation caused by the apartheid state’s wars and destabilisation of neighbouring countries, including Namibia, Angola and Mozambique.

But we must be clear that, within South Africa itself, the apartheid state did not carry out mass killing on the scale that we have witnessed with the genocide in Gaza. Recognising this difference does not diminish the suffering of South Africans under apartheid.

In South Africa, formal apartheid ended in 1994 when the Black majority finally won the right to vote and the country elected a democratic government. A single country was formed in which there was a single democracy with one person, one vote.

But the Palestinian people have not yet won their freedom. There has been no equivalent democratic settlement that recognises their full and equal humanity and political rights. There must also be a single free and democratic country with equal rights for all and one person, one vote in historic Palestine, from the river to the sea.

Of course in South Africa we have been betrayed by the ANC who have enriched themselves, repressed popular movements and struggles and left a devastated country with mass impoverishment, mass hunger and mass unemployment, including more than 60% youth unemployment. The ANC failed to deal with the structural basis of oppression. They did not even undertake meaningful land reform. South Africa shows both that the achievement of a single democratic state is possible, and that betrayal by new leaders and elites is also possible, with the result that it is essential for people to remain organised before, during and after liberation.

In South Africa, apartheid was defeated by a powerful trade union movement, a mass uprising of the people and the defeat of the apartheid military by the Cubans in Angola. A small but often brave minority of white people also opposed the system, weakening the white bloc in support of apartheid.

The different nature of oppression in Palestine and the different world situation means that a powerful trade union movement, a mass popular uprising and a defeat of the Israeli military by a socialist government is impossible. And while there are some Israelis who oppose the oppression of Palestinians, some with real courage, they are a very small minority and have not been able to weaken the fascist bloc in Israel.

Solidarity Between Our Struggles

There is a long history of solidarity between the South African and Palestinian liberation movements. The African National Congress (ANC), the Palestine Liberation Organisation, the Irish Republican Army and the Polisario Front all understand themselves as national liberation movements in a shared struggle against settler colonial oppression.

The ANC remains in solidarity with the Palestinian struggle, as do the vast majority of the South African people, including our movement and the trade unions.

Our movement was formed in Durban in 2005 by people living in shack settlements who had become tired of waiting for the promises of freedom to be fulfilled. We were told that apartheid had ended and that we were now free. But we continued to live without secure access to land, decent housing, water, electricity and sanitation.

We faced evictions and forced removals. Our homes were demolished. People were pushed away from the cities to places where there were no jobs and few opportunities to build a decent life. We discovered that the poor were still expected to know their place.

We were expected to accept decisions made by politicians and officials without participating in those decisions. We were treated as people who should be told what to do by others, such as the government, the ruling party and some NGOs, rather than as people who could think, organise and determine our own future.

When we insisted on our right to organise ourselves and speak for ourselves, we faced severe repression, including assassinations and police killings. Twenty-six lives have been lost in the course of our struggle.

Our movement rejected this. We insisted that the poor are human beings who can think for ourselves, speak for ourselves and organise ourselves. We have always said that the land and wealth of our country must be shared, that every person must count as a person, and that no one should be treated as if their life has less value than another.

We know what it means to have your home destroyed. We know what it means to be forced from land on which you have built your life. We know what it means to be confronted by armed men when you are simply demanding the right to live in dignity. We know what it is like to be tortured and to have our comrades murdered.

This is also why we understand the suffering of the Palestinian people. Our solidarity with Palestine is not based on the idea that our suffering is identical. It is based on the recognition that the oppression of another human being is a matter of concern to all of us. We are in solidarity with all oppressed people everywhere, from Palestine to the Congo, to migrants in the United States and our LGBTI comrades facing persecution in many countries.

We have faced severe repression from the ANC, and have been involved in a bitter struggle against them, our new oppressors. However, when the South African government brought its case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in December 2023, we offered our full support for this action.

We were proud when South African lawyers stood before the Court in The Hague and presented the case that Israel’s actions in Gaza violated the Genocide Convention. We regarded this as an important act of international solidarity and a defence of the humanity of the Palestinian people.

Any principled politics supports all measures to oppose oppression and we were clear that we must support this action of the ANC in government. However, it is very disappointing that South Africa continues to sell coal to Israel, is exploring for oil and gas in our oceans with an Israeli company and that ANC-aligned trade unions have not refused to load coal onto ships heading to Israel or refused to handle any ships heading to Israel as dockworkers in Namibia, Italy and elsewhere have done.

In 2025, South Africa exported approximately 1.8 million tonnes of coal to Israel. When the progressive government in Colombia stopped exporting coal to Israel, South Africa increased its shipments. This is very disappointing and must be clearly opposed.

The Problem of Race and Class in Palestine Solidarity Networks

The vast majority of South African people feel a deep kinship with the Palestinian people. This solidarity is rooted in our history. We know what it means to experience colonial domination, racial oppression, dispossession and the denial of human dignity. The Palestinian struggle has a particular meaning for South Africans because so many of us recognise aspects of our own history in the suffering of Palestinians.

But we must be honest about a serious failure in the solidarity networks in South Africa. This widespread solidarity felt by the majority of the South African people has not been effectively mobilised into the kind of powerful popular movement that could make South Africa a much stronger force in support of Palestine.

The reason for this is the failure to confront questions of race and class within the Palestine solidarity movement in South Africa itself. Poor and working-class African people have been systematically excluded from international connections and from participation in the decision-making in the wider solidarity movement. When we have been included, it has often been in subordinate, patronising and disrespectful ways. It is often assumed that our only job is to fill buses to make up the numbers at protests in which we have no role in planning. This is a serious political problem that has seriously weakened the solidarity movement.

If we want South Africa’s solidarity with Palestine to become a powerful popular force, the movement must be rooted much more deeply in the lives, struggles and organisations of the African working class and poor. We need to be engaged with respect and not just treated as people who must always be instructed by others, and often in very disrespectful ways. To be effective, the movement must be built through relationships of equality and mutual respect. Until these problems are confronted, the enormous potential of South African solidarity with the Palestinian people will remain largely unrealised.

The Power of International Solidarity

Our movement is very encouraged by the re-election of Lula in Brazil and by the recent political successes of the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, including the election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York City. But in many countries, particularly in Latin America, left-wing governments have lost power and the right has advanced. In Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and other countries, right-wing forces have made major gains.

South Africa is also experiencing a dramatic shift to the right. In our recent local government elections, the African National Congress suffered an extraordinary defeat, while right-wing parties made major gains. Some of these parties are openly hostile to migrants and have supported aggressive forms of nationalism and xenophobia. Some are also strongly in support of Israel.

In the current conjuncture Israel will not be defeated by states. It can, though, be defeated by the people of the world. In Aotearoa, the movement against the Springbok tour demonstrated that ordinary people could challenge a powerful system of oppression even when their own government was unwilling to take the necessary action.

We have been greatly encouraged by the solidarity that has been developed around the world, from the students in the United States to the dockworkers who, on 30 October this year, organised coordinated strikes and demonstrations at more than one hundred ports around the world against war, the transport of weapons and the militarisation of ports. Workers from Europe, North Africa and other parts of the world joined this mobilisation, with solidarity for Palestine at its centre.

The people of the world are called, with great urgency, to be in meaningful solidarity with the people of Palestine. This is a great mission of our generation and we cannot betray our responsibilities.

From the river to the sea, Palestine must be free.

author: Abahlali_3
title: Socialism or Barbarism?
content:
Keynote address at the Third National Conference of the Aotearoa New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies held in Ōtepoti Dunedin, on Saturday, 14 November 2026.

Comrade Programme director, thank you for welcoming me to Aotearoa once again. May I express my sincere gratitude to the New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies and Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa for inviting me to speak here today, and across the country. I bring greetings from Abahlali baseMjondolo, our movement in South Africa which now has more than 200,000 members.

I want to begin with the words of a song, a song about socialism, that is often sung in the struggles of the left in South Africa.

Yini iSocialism? Umhlaba wonke ezandleni zabantu Akunamuntu, akunamuntu ongaphatha umhlaba ngayedwa Ayayesaba bo, ayesaba amabhujwa, nongxiwa Ngoba bona, ngobabona befuna ukusetshenzelwa ngabantu

The song asks, ‘What is socialism?’ It answers that socialism is the whole world in the hands of the people. It goes on to say that no one person can own the world on their own. It concludes that the bourgeoisie are afraid of socialism, because they want the people to work for them.

Comrades, as you will all know, in 1915, during the mass slaughter of the First World War, Rosa Luxemburg wrote from a prison cell in Germany that humanity stood at a crossroads. Either it would move towards socialism, towards global justice and peace, or it would collapse into further barbarism. She was writing as millions of workers were being sent to kill each other in the trenches for the profits of their rulers. Four years later she was murdered.

In our movement we have our own version of this choice. Lindokuhle Mnguni, the gifted young chairperson of one of our branches, the eKhenana Commune in Durban, introduced the slogan ‘Socialism or Death’ into our movement. For Lindokuhle, socialism was not something that would come one day in the future, after a revolution, or after an election. Socialism had to be lived now, in the way we occupy land, ensure that it is not bought and sold, manage it democratically, grow food together, ensure that nobody goes hungry, care for each other, build and manage social infrastructure like halls, creches and kitchens, and make decisions together.

For us, like urban and rural movements elsewhere in the world, building socialism from below means building communes, connecting them and building wider forms of democratic popular power from these communes. In the same way that the liberated zones were the bases for anti-colonial movements in countries like Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau, communes – from South Africa to Brazil, Venezuela and elsewhere – are the strongest bases for our movements to build socialism. As Ruthie Wilson Gilmore says, ‘Freedom is a place’.

The price for challenging oppression can be very high. Many comrades around the world have given their lives. On 20 August 2022, Lindokuhle was shot dead in his home. He was the third leader of the eKhenana Commune to be assassinated in less than six months.

Frantz Fanon taught that ‘Each generation must, out of relative obscurity, discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it.’ Comrades like Rosa Luxemburg and Lindokuhle Mnguni understood the mission of their generation, and gave their lives to it. Our generation also has a mission. We are living in a time of genocide, of wealth beyond imagination for a few and hunger for millions, of the far right and fascist forces rising and of the poor being turned against each other. We have to decide whether we will fulfil our mission or betray it. In our movement we have often used Fanon’s words. When people find themselves pushed to the margins of the city and of life, they have the opportunity to discover their mission and to decide whether they want to fulfil it or betray it.

I want to speak today about the barbarism that we see around us, in South Africa and around the world, and about the work of building socialism from below, as we have tried to do it in our movement.

When Luxemburg wrote about barbarism she was thinking of the slaughter of the First World War. Today we are witnessing another mass slaughter of human beings. We have all watched the genocide in Gaza. We have watched children being starved, hospitals and schools being bombed, and whole families being buried under the rubble of their homes. We have watched the most powerful governments in the world supply the weapons and protect Israel at the United Nations. We have watched the liberal governments of the West back Israel and turn on their own citizens when they have stood up for truth and justice. In the United Kingdom, Peter Hallward, a comrade who stood up for us when we were facing violent repression from the ANC in 2009, was arrested and charged with terrorism for holding up a placard at a demonstration in solidarity with the Palestinian people.

There are many kinds of barbarism. We must not hesitate to say that the economic system – capitalism – that makes the rich to be rich and the poor to be poor is barbaric. In January this year it was reported that the wealth of the world’s billionaires had reached 18.3 trillion US dollars, the highest level in history. Their wealth grew by 2.5 trillion dollars in 2025 alone. That increase in one year is almost equal to all the wealth of the poorest half of humanity, more than four billion people. At the same time nearly half of the people in the world live in poverty, and one person in four does not regularly have enough to eat. There are now more than 3,000 billionaires.

This world in which a few thousand people own more wealth than billions of others was made, and it is maintained by force. In our movement we say that we were made poor so that others could be made rich, and that we are kept poor so that others can remain rich. This is why we insist on a world in which land, wealth and power are shared, a world in which every person counts as a person.

In South Africa we won our democracy in 1994. But the poor are now greater in number, and poorer, than they were in 1994, while the rich have become richer and richer. Millions of people still live in shacks. Youth unemployment is at 60% and millions of young people have never had a job. When people organise to demand land, housing and dignity they are evicted, arrested and sometimes killed. Twenty-six of our comrades have lost their lives in the course of our struggle. Some were murdered by the police. Some were murdered by hired killers working for local politicians. Two ANC councillors are serving life sentences for the murder of our comrade Thuli Ndlovu, who was shot dead in her home in 2014 while she was helping a child with homework.

There is another kind of barbarism that comes when the poor and the working class are turned against each other. Everywhere in the world the oppressed are being divided. Xenophobia is the greatest weapon unleashed against the oppressed, but we are also divided by race, by religion in some countries, as well as by language, culture and ethnicity.

The system needs us to believe that our neighbours are taking our jobs and our houses. It needs us to look down at people who are as poor as we are rather than up at the people who are getting rich from our suffering. The crisis in our hospitals is caused by austerity, mismanagement and corruption. There is mass unemployment because we have an economy that was built on extraction and exclusion and that has never broken with its colonial origins.

This is not only a South African problem. Across the world right-wing forces are scapegoating migrants for the devastation caused by capitalism. We see it in Europe. We see it in the United States, where migrants are being hunted by ICE. In South Africa some of the parties that gained votes in our recent local government elections are extremely hostile to migrants. Some of these same parties support Israel.

In India Muslims are made into the enemy. In Europe and the United States it is migrants and refugees. In South Africa it is people from Asia and other African countries, and increasingly South Africans who speak minority languages. Each time, the people who are made into enemies are as poor as the people who are told to hate them. Each time, the people who own the land, the mines, the banks and the media are left untouched. Each time the politicians who steal from the people are left untouched. In 2020 we ended a statement against xenophobia with the words Sazi isitha sakho, know your enemy.

To resist this division, and to build the unity of the oppressed, the working class and the poor, is one of the most urgent tasks of our time. Without that unity there can be no socialism.

Today even people who see themselves as workers move between being employed and being impoverished. This is why the unity of the working class and the impoverished is necessary if we are to win the battle against the forces that we are all against. Fanon wrote that when the people come to understand their situation they realise that everything depends on them, and that their salvation lies in their own unity and courage, in the true understanding of their interests and in knowing who their enemies are.

For our movement this work of building togetherness begins with the recognition of the humanity of every person. There is only one human race. A person is a person wherever they find themselves. A neighbour is a neighbour and a comrade is a comrade wherever they may come from. Our humanity cannot be judged by where we were born, by the language that we speak or by how much money we have.

Dignity is the ethical core of our politics. The dignity of human beings is universal and non-negotiable, and it is the point from which resistance is built. When we diminish or vandalise the humanity of others we disgrace our own humanity. Hatred of this kind always weakens the poor and the working-class people, and so it has to be rejected by poor and working-class people first.

In May 2008 a wave of xenophobic violence spread across South Africa. At least 62 people were killed and more than 100,000 were driven from their homes. Our movement held a careful discussion over two days, and on 21 May we issued a statement. We said that there is only one human race. We said that an action can be illegal, but a person cannot be illegal. We said, in isiZulu, Unyawo alunampumulo, that a person is a person wherever they may find themselves. We sheltered and defended people who were under attack.

Before 2008 we had spoken a great deal about the dignity of our own members. In 2008 we had to affirm that we were committed to the dignity of everyone.

In 2025 the courts found that Operation Dudula, an organisation that had been blocking migrants from hospitals and attacking them in the streets, was acting in a way that was unlawful and unconstitutional. Operation Dudula is a violent, fascist organisation that uses military uniforms. When they marched on the offices of the Socio-Economic Rights Institute in Johannesburg, the law firm that has represented our movement and many migrants, hundreds of our members stood on the streets to defend the Socio-Economic Rights Institute. When Operation Dudula arrived, they found themselves vastly outnumbered by our members, and they left. Every human being is called to resist fascism and there can be no socialism that is not also anti-fascist.

This year there has been a terrible new wave of organised xenophobic violence in South Africa. In KwaZulu-Natal armed mobs have gone from house to house driving people from their homes, businesses and workplaces. They say that they are just demanding that the laws against illegal migration are enforced but they have repeatedly and openly attacked documented migrants too, including refugees. More than 150,000 people were forced out of the country in a few weeks. As our General Secretary, Thapelo Mohapi, has warned, this kind of violence always starts with the outsider and ends with the minority at home. What we are witnessing has a name and that name is fascism. We draw a line, a red line, against fascism when we insist that every person is a person no matter who and where they are.

In 2020, when I spoke to the United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, I said that our politics needs to develop a living communism, a politic in which every person counts as a person and the dignity of every human being is respected.

Ubuntu, ubuhlalism and socialism

Our own movement was born out of a struggle to be counted as human beings. For years we had been told that we were free, but we did not count in this society. We were not recognised as human beings. Our suffering did not count as human suffering. Our lives did not count as human lives.

Our movement was born in 2005 in a shack settlement called Kennedy Road in Durban. We had been promised land near our settlement for housing. Then we discovered that the land had been sold to a businessman for a brick factory. In March 2005 we blockaded a main road, and many of us were beaten and arrested. We realised that if we wanted to be counted as human beings, we would have to organise ourselves.

From the beginning we insisted that the poor can think for ourselves, speak for ourselves and organise for ourselves. Neighbouring communities saw that our demands were their demands, and they joined us. Together we built a politics of the poor, a homemade politics that everyone can understand and find a home in. We decided that we would think and speak for ourselves and not be told what to do by politicians, by the ruling party or by NGOs. Our meetings were, and remain, open to everyone. Leaders are elected, they must remain accountable to the people, and they can be recalled. A leader is a tool of the people. For our oppressors the people are the tools of the leaders. Our first battles were to defend our settlements from eviction and to win basic services. Over time, as the state destroyed our homes and refused to give us land, we began to occupy unused land ourselves. This is land reform from below, urban planning from below. Land and dignity became central commitments in our movement.

In South Africa we speak of ubuntu, the idea that umuntu ungumuntu ngabantu, a person is a person through other people. It is not often admitted that ubuntu has not always been intended to apply to all people. We have radicalised ubuntu by insisting that it applies to every human being everywhere. For us ubuntu is a practice that demonstrates, builds and defends our shared humanity. In our communities, when a family fell on hard times, another family would lend them livestock. This is what ubuntu meant in practice.

In 2012 our movement spent a whole day in discussion about socialism and communism. Many of us were drawn to these ideas. But socialism often came to us through small sectarian organisations and NGOs, and communism through the South African Communist Party, which is part of the ruling alliance, which was silent while we were being oppressed and is now working with xenophobic and corrupt forces. It seemed to us that both were leaving us out. So, we decided to give our own name to our politics. We called it ubuhlali, the politics of abahlali, the residents, and we rooted it in ubuntu. We spend a great deal of time in our political education on ubuntu, because unless we are responsible human beings who love our fellow human beings, we will not win the battle for justice and equality. This is the most important part of our work, and it comes before we engage in our struggles for land, housing and dignity. We have also spoken of a living politic, a politics that everyone can understand and take part in, that comes from our lives and does not belong to experts. Later we began to speak of a living communism, a communism that emerges from the lives and struggles of the oppressed.

Our road to socialism began with ubuntu. Ubuntu led us to ubuhlali, and ubuhlali led us to democratic socialism from below. It is important to understand that we did not come to humanism from socialism, it was the other way around. We came to socialism from humanism, from the insistence that every human being must count as a human being.

Later we found that in 1844 the young Karl Marx wrote that ‘communism … equals humanism’. In 1960 Léopold Sédar Senghor, the poet who became the first president of Senegal, said, ‘Our socialism is a humanism.’ For us the political form that humanism must take is socialism, and our socialism must always remain a humanism.

When I spoke on UnFreedom Day in 2018 I said that we are struggling for umbuso we socialism lapho wonke umhlaba, nomnotho wezwe uzolawulwa ngabahlali nabasebenzi, a socialist order in which all the land and all the wealth of the country will be controlled by the residents and workers.

We have learnt that if you begin with a debate about capitalism and socialism in the abstract you can confuse people on the ground. Politics starts with the everyday lives of people. So, we begin with what people are living, with homelessness, with land and food, with the lack of water and electricity, and with the way that people are treated by the police and by the councillors. When people ask why a family in a middle-class suburb can have seven taps in one house while thousands of us share a handful of toilets, the discussion about racism, political betrayal and capitalism has already begun. Then we can explain the system, how the system of private property degrades the lives of millions to benefit a few. You have to start with what people understand and then build the theory together. You can have brilliant ideas, but if they are detached from the people, they will make no difference to the world.

Rosa Luxemburg understood this. In December 1918, a few weeks before she was murdered, she wrote that the transformation of society ‘cannot be decreed by any bureau, committee, or parliament. It can be begun and carried out only by the masses of people themselves.’ The people, she said, must ‘bring socialism step by step into life’. This is why we say that we are a socialist organisation committed to building socialism from below through the construction of popular democratic power.

When ideas come from the people, are discussed, thought through and returned to the people, they can become very powerful. In 2019, thousands of our members marched through Durban to demand the total decommodification of land. For many years our members had been saying umhlaba noma ukufa, land or death, and many have given their lives in the struggle for land. This demand for the total decommodification of land came out of months of discussion in our branches. We said that land is not a commodity. Land must be allocated on the basis of human need rather than private profit, and it must be managed collectively and democratically by the people who live on it. The social value of land must come before its commercial value.

People sometimes ask us where our socialism comes from. It comes from our lives, from thinking about our lives together, although some of us have also read many books.

Our movement was formed on 4 October 2005 at a meeting of 32 people. Today we have more than 200,000 members. Over the last twenty-one years we have learnt some things about how to build a movement. I would like to share some of these things in case they are useful.

There is no emancipatory politics without listening to others. To lead people is to listen to them, because the people will tell you what to do. When our comrades go to a new community to run political education, they do not bring a programme. They go to listen, to hear what the comrades want to learn. When there is a crisis, we hold assemblies and we listen to everyone, very carefully, before we take a position. Every time you listen to another person you have the opportunity to learn from them. We build our humanity through listening.

A movement must also recognise and support the humanity of its own members now, while it struggles for a world in which the humanity of everyone is recognised. When people come to us the first questions are whether they will be respected and how they will be respected. We come together to develop and defend our humanity and our dignity, and to make the world more human. Our meetings are open to everyone and everyone can speak. When a comrade is sick, we visit them. When a comrade is killed, we bury them with the dignity that they were denied in life. A person who is suffering needs to know that they are not alone. A movement that does not treat its own members as human beings cannot build a more human world.

Building a movement takes courage. Courage has to be built together and sustained together. We must encourage each other.

Building a movement also takes healing. In South Africa we all come out of a history of serious violence, from colonialism and apartheid, to the civil war in KwaZulu-Natal, to the repression that we face today. Other countries have their own histories of oppression and suffering. Without an honest conversation about how to heal together, we will remain unable to build a human form of politics.

Perhaps our most important achievement has been to change the way that people think about themselves. The state creates dependency and division in order to control people. We have built trust and solidarity among the poor; we have built the confidence of the oppressed. When people know that they can resist and win, even if the victories are small, it changes everything.

Leaders must be humble; they must take the ideas of the people seriously and they must remain accountable. When you have to speak for people you have to do justice to the people. Sometimes it is better to be wrong with the people than to be right without the people.

Communities must own the movement, not the leadership. When leaders begin to feel entitled to money or to the assets of the movement, the movement must be strong enough to stop them.

A movement must also protect its autonomy. A movement that gives up its autonomy to a political party or an NGO will quickly collapse.

But autonomy does not mean isolation. No movement can win on its own. It is very important for movements to work with other movements, and with progressive churches, trade unions, lawyers and intellectuals, on the basis of equality and mutual respect.

We have marched with trade unions, with street traders and with organised migrants. Today we stand with the South African Federation of Trade Unions in taking a principled line against xenophobia.

We have had wonderful relationships with some academics, who have worked with us with humility and respect for many years, and good relationships with many progressive organisations of different kinds. But we have also had very bad and damaging experiences with some academics and NGOs. Some of them thought that their role was to think for poor people. This included liberals, and also the kind of leftists who see their role as giving political direction to the oppressed rather than working with the oppressed on the basis of mutual respect. When we insisted on taking our direction from our own members some of them became openly hostile to us.

When we refused to be treated as people who cannot think, some said that someone else must be thinking for us, that we were being controlled from behind. This is a very old racist idea about black people who struggle for their freedom. It has done great damage to the left in South Africa, and we sometimes hear about the same kind of thing in other countries.

Mutual respect is the only basis on which a powerful left can be built. Unity between movements and other organisations must be built in cities, in countries and across the world. We are part of a global movement of movements and always work to build internationalism. Some people are surprised when they come to our meetings and hear how beautifully our choir sings the Internationale. They should not be. Internationalism is for all of humanity.

We will end as we began. Yini iSocialism? Socialism is all of the world in the hands of the people.

All of us here today, all of us in this room have made the same choice. We have chosen socialism over barbarism. Now our task is to work together to fulfil our mission.

title: We mourn the loss of Des D’sa
content:
30 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo press statement

We mourn the loss of Des D’Sa, father, uncle, grandfather, and a comrade to many

The death of Desmond D’Sa has plunged many people on the left in Durban and beyond, across numerous organisations, into shock and despair. Siyakhala ngo Des.

Comrade Des was a stalwart in the struggle against apartheid and was a well-known organiser who formed the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA), an environmental organisation that raised the concerns of families living in the oil- and gas-affected areas of Wentworth and the Bluff.

His activism and the fight against injustices did not end with environmental issues and it definitely did not end in Wentworth and the Bluff. Comrade Des fought against all forms of oppression and injustice, including gangsterism and the mining companies in rural areas, and supported everyone from fisherfolk to migrants and poor people, whether living in flats, hostels or shacks. He did not back down when struggle became dangerous. Comrade Des spoke fluent isiZulu and engaged everyone with the same respect.

title: Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer
content:
25 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer

Our country is one of the most violent in the world, worse than some war zones. The rate of violence against women and the rate of murders committed by young men against other young men are among the highest in the world. There is violence in the home and in communities, violence from ordinary people, politicians, criminals and the armed forces in service of the state and the rich.

Our country and its people have been deeply damaged by generations of oppression, which has continued into the present for many people, especially the poor. The ANC has never pursued a project of healing, a project of restoring the humanity of our people and our society. They have just made themselves rich, leaving most of us poor and living in a broken society, a broken society in which the poor continue to be ruled with violence.

Things are getting worse. In KwaZulu-Natal armed mobs now parade through the streets accompanied by the police. People have been driven from their homes and livelihoods, assaulted and killed. The rise of the right, including violent fascist organisations, is a matter of grave concern for our movement and all people of good conscience.
